sheet-2.description: Sheet 2, drawn at 100 ft to an inch, covers the north-west residential district of the borough, from the curving roads at the top of the sheet down to Stockton Street, and from open ground at the left to Bayard Lane at the right. Hodge Road crosses the sheet from lower left to upper right and then runs east to Bayard Lane; Cleveland Lane curves off it to the north and returns to Bayard Lane. Library Place runs south from Hodge Road to Stockton Street, and Morven and Boudinot Street lie between Library Place and Bayard Lane. The district is one of large lots, many of them numbered but still empty: lots 32 to 58 along the top curves and Cleveland Lane are mostly unbuilt. Built lots hold large frame, brick and stone dwellings, many stuccoed, with automobile houses, stables and a green house; a portable forge and repair shop stands in block 3 at the upper left. The largest building is the Princeton Inn (Princeton Inn Co., L. H. MacDowell, manager) in block 11 between Boudinot and Stockton, with a boiler house, servants' quarters and a printed note on its fire protection; the Peacock Inn stands on Bayard Lane at its corner with Boudinot. Short stubs of Greenholm Street, Nassau Street and Mercer Street appear at the right and lower right edges, and Edgehill Street meets Stockton at the bottom. Water pipes with their laying dates are drawn along most streets. A compass rose and the scale bar fill the open ground at the left, where block 10 holds only a few scattered buildings.
notes: Hodge Road is lettered with its alternative name in brackets, 'Hodge (Hodge Av.) Rd'.
The eastern stretch of Cleveland Lane toward Bayard Lane is lettered '(A St.)'.
Greenholm St., a stub off Bayard Lane at the right edge, has no street of that name in the modern reference data.
Princeton Inn (Princeton Inn Co., L. H. MacDowell, manager) occupies block 11 between Boudinot and Stockton.
The Peacock Inn stands on Bayard Lane at Boudinot.
Many lots are numbered but empty, especially along Cleveland Lane and the curved roads at the top.

100 ft. Northwest: Hodge Rd, Cleveland Ln, Library Pl, Boudinot, Morven Pl, Bayard Ln, Stockton. Automatic detection; the hand-picked points in manual/sheet-2.json were 13-40 ft off (checked at full res) and are not used.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3, at 50 ft to an inch, covers the ground between Bayard Lane on the west and John Street on the east, from the end of Hodge Road at the top down to Nassau Street at the bottom. The upper half is the Greenholm estate: a few large dwellings, one of hollow tile, stand among open grounds crossed by an oval double drive with lots numbered 301 to 322 along it. The lower half is a dense block of streets running north from Nassau Street. Bank Street and Chambers Street are lined with small two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings and several boarding houses. Along Nassau Street, from west to east, are a large garage and machine shop of corrugated iron, a gasoline pump, an auto supplies and tire repair building, a meat market, The Princeton Bank, a furniture and carpets store, then the Second Presbyterian Church with its Sunday school and tower at Chambers Street. East of the church, toward John Street, stand concrete-floored buildings with a drug store, telephone exchange, photographer, tailor, florist and other shops, and further up John Street a second-hand furniture store, a tailor and clothes cleaning shop and a hay, feed and grain and furniture storage building. The fire department house, with hose carriages and a 28 ft tower, stands on Chambers Street. Boudinot Street, Stockton Street and Mercer Street appear as stubs at the left and bottom edges, University Place at the bottom, and Green Street, Jackson Street and Hulfish Street as stubs on John Street at the right. The scale bar and a compass rose fill open ground.
notes: Jackson St., a stub on John Street at the right edge, is now Paul Robeson Place.
The Greenholm estate fills the upper half; its oval drive carries lot numbers 301 to 322.
Second Presbyterian Church with Sunday school stands at Chambers and Nassau.
The fire department house (hose carriages, 28 ft tower) is on Chambers Street.
The Princeton Bank is on Nassau Street between Bank and Chambers.
50 ft. Bayard Ln, Bank, Chambers, Nassau, John; Greenholm estate (NE quarter) has no control. Bank/Chambers and Chambers/John are merged/realigned modern nodes, excluded.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4, at 50 ft to an inch, is turned about 90 degrees on the page, with north pointing to the left. It covers the north end of the borough along Witherspoon, which runs across the top of the sheet as drawn, with John crossing the middle and Lytle along the right side. Between them, from left to right, lie a trolley right of way, block 17, block 18, Leigh Avenue, block 19, Clay and block 20; Birch Avenue runs down the lower left between blocks 14 and 15. Most of the sheet is laid out in narrow numbered lots, many still empty, especially the long rows in blocks 15 and 18 and below John. Built lots hold small one- and two-storey frame dwellings, flats, a few stores (groceries, a barber, a cabinet maker) and sheds, with the densest building along Witherspoon near Lytle and in block 20 between Clay and Lytle. Block 17, beside the trolley right of way, holds the corn crusher, slaughter house and barns of A. S. Leigh, with an iron water cylinder, corn cribs, a hay house, a wagon house, a contractor's store house and an ice house; coal bins with no roof are drawn along the trolley line. A dash-dot borough line crosses the sheet between Leigh Avenue and Clay, from Witherspoon down across John. Franklin Avenue and Witherspoon Lane appear only as stubs at the top margin. Clay is drawn ending short of Witherspoon. A row of eight brick dwellings, numbers 152 to 166, fronts John just right of the borough line. The lower right is open ground in block 16, with the compass rose.
notes: A dash-dot line lettered 'Borough Line' crosses the sheet between Leigh Avenue and Clay.
A trolley right of way runs along the left (north) edge of the sheet, with coal bins beside it.
A. S. Leigh corn crusher, slaughter house and barns occupy block 17.
The street between blocks 17 and 18, parallel to Leigh Avenue, is not lettered.
Franklin Avenue and Witherspoon Lane are drawn only as stubs at the top edge.
50 ft. Turned about 90 degrees on the page (north points left). Witherspoon, Leigh Av, Birch Av, Clay, Lytle, John. Clay did not reach Witherspoon in 1911.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5, at 50 ft to an inch, covers the residential district between John on the west and Witherspoon on the east, from Lytle at the top down to Green at the bottom, with MacLean and Quarry crossing between them. A strip west of John and a strip east of Witherspoon are also drawn. Its institutions are labelled: the Witherspoon Public School (Colored), a brick building with a manual training room on Quarry; the Mount Pisgah A.M.E. Church and an Odd Fellows Hall on Witherspoon at MacLean; Douglas Hall on Witherspoon near Lytle; and the Witherspoon Presbyterian Church with its parish house on Witherspoon at Quarry, with the Men's Association of the church at the corner of Green. Otherwise the blocks hold small two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, some flats, several groceries, a coal and wood shed, sheds and stables. Block 22 between MacLean and Quarry has a large open interior. At the top right Witherspoon Lane leaves Witherspoon eastward, with a bakery and iron oven beside it. East of Witherspoon the lots back onto ground lettered Cemetery Addition, where two small buildings stand in the open. The lower part of the sheet below Green is left blank: it belongs to sheet 6, and only the sheet number, a library stamp and the scale bar are drawn there. A compass rose stands at the right.
notes: Witherspoon Lane is lettered 'Witherspoon (Onque) Lane'.
Mac Lean is the modern Maclean Street.
Witherspoon Public School (Colored) stands on Quarry in block 22.
Mount Pisgah A.M.E. Church, Odd Fellows Hall and Douglas Hall are on Witherspoon; the Witherspoon Presbyterian Church and its parish house are at Quarry.
The area below Green is blank; it is drawn on sheet 6.
50 ft. Lytle, MacLean, Quarry, Green, John, Witherspoon.

sheet-6-main.description: The main part of sheet 6, at 50 ft to an inch, covers the block of the town centre between John on the west and Witherspoon on the east, from Green at the top down to Nassau at the bottom, with Jackson and Hulfish crossing between them and Nassau Place and Baker running north from Nassau. Its western edge is the heavy line beside the railroad; the Alexander Street strip beyond it is a separate part. The upper blocks (25 and 26) between Green, Jackson and Hulfish are residential: small frame dwellings in narrow lots, the Bright Hope Baptist Church on John, the Charles Z. Page monumental works near Witherspoon, and a borough of Princeton lock-up. Block 28 below Hulfish holds liveries, carriage sheds, painting and repair shops, a cabinet maker and upholsterer, and an iron-clad garage with repair and machine shops on Nassau Place. Block 27 between Baker and Witherspoon is the commercial edge of the centre: Hotel Higgins, pool rooms, a tin shop, barbers, a bakery, a boys' club, the fire department house with its fire bell on an iron tower, the Witherspoon Hotel and an ice cream factory. The Nassau frontage is solid brick: the Nassau Inn (J. B. Renwick, proprietor) with its kitchen, dining room, bar and office, a savings bank, cycle repairing, sporting goods, stationery, men's furnishings, confectioners, drugs, and the First National Bank at the Witherspoon corner. Wiggins Street and Spring Street appear as stubs east of Witherspoon at the right edge. A compass rose stands beside Witherspoon.
notes: Jackson is now Paul Robeson Place.
Nassau Place and Baker no longer exist; their blocks were rebuilt as Palmer Square.
Nassau Inn (J. B. Renwick, proprietor) fronts Nassau west of Nassau Place.
First National Bank stands at the corner of Nassau and Witherspoon.
Bright Hope Baptist Church is on John between Green and Jackson.
Fire department house, Witherspoon Hotel and Hotel Higgins are on Witherspoon.

50 ft. Two parts: main (John to Witherspoon, Green to Nassau; old John/Jackson corner replaced by Palmer Square, helmert along Witherspoon) and Alexander St strip with the railroad west of x~483 (no junction, not configured).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: Alexander Street with the lumber yard and the PRR Princeton branch (no street junction (Alexander only, railroad parallel); the 1911 branch line differs from the modern track; needs step 6b from a placed neighbour sharing the rail spur (sheet-17 strips, once placed) or sheet-13).

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7, at 50 ft to an inch, is drawn with north pointing to the left. It covers the blocks between Witherspoon, along the bottom as drawn, and Nassau, along the right side, reaching up to Madison at the top; Wiggins runs down the left side. Van Deventer Avenue and Park divide the upper half, and North Tulane, South Tulane, Spring and Lincoln Court the lower half. The upper blocks (30, 31 and 33) are residential, with large two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings and automobile houses on Madison, Van Deventer Avenue and Park; the Princeton M.E. Church with its Sunday school stands on Nassau at Van Deventer Avenue, and the Public Library and Town Club just below it. Block 34, between Wiggins, North Tulane, Spring and Witherspoon, is mostly empty numbered lots except for the works of the Public Service Gas and Electric Company on Witherspoon: two gasometers, retort house, coal shed, storage, dynamo room and meter room. The rest of Witherspoon is commercial: furniture, rugs and carpets, a tailor, Benham House, a newspaper and freight house, an ice cream factory, a moving picture house with a basket ball court above, a livery, laundries and the Central Hotel. The Nassau frontage holds the Prospect Inn, wallpaper, harness, cobbler, cleaning, jewellery, meat, grocery and saloon stores, a Chinese laundry, offices and the post office, with lodge rooms behind. Lincoln Court has bowling alleys, and a large garage of corrugated iron stands off South Tulane. Stubs of Humbert Street, Greenview Avenue, Jackson Street, Hulfish Street and Washington Road appear at the edges.
notes: Spring is lettered 'Spring (Spring Garden)'; it is the modern Spring Street.
Van Deventer Avenue is the modern Vandeventer Avenue.
Jackson Street, a stub at the bottom edge, is now Paul Robeson Place.
Public Service Gas and Electric Company works with two gasometers stand on Witherspoon.
Princeton M.E. Church and the Public Library and Town Club are on Nassau.
The post office is at the corner of Nassau and Witherspoon; the Central Hotel is on Witherspoon.
50 ft. North points left. Madison, Vandeventer, Tulane, Spring, Park Pl, Wiggins, Witherspoon, Nassau. Pilot sheet. Paul Robeson Pl node excluded (realigned).

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8, at 50 ft to an inch, is drawn with north pointing to the left. It covers the area between Chestnut along the top as drawn and Madison along the bottom, from Wiggins at the left to Nassau at the right. Moran Avenue runs below Chestnut, and Moore crosses the lower half, with Willow, Park and Branch Avenue between Moore and Madison. The middle of the sheet is block 36, most of it a large cemetery. Beside it, toward Nassau, stand St. Paul's R.C. Church, its parish hall, St. Paul's School, a priests' house and a convent. Between Chestnut and Moran Avenue is a row of narrow lots with small frame dwellings and outbuildings, including a few stores and shops. Below Moore, block 35 between Wiggins and Willow holds two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, the University Laundry Co. (steam power, wash room and engine room with a 60 ft chimney) and the carpenter and cabinet shop of V. F. Frohling. Between Willow and Park are frame dwellings and a carpenter's shop, and on Branch Avenue the G. C. Silcox planing mill with a gasoline engine. Block 31 between Park and Nassau is residential, with an undertaking shop and automobile houses. Stubs of Spruce Street, Olden Street, Charlton Street, Hamilton Avenue and Jefferson Road appear at the edges. A compass rose stands in the cemetery and the scale bar at the lower right.
notes: The cemetery in block 36 is lettered only 'Cemetery'.
St. Paul's R.C. Church, parish hall, St. Paul's School and a convent stand beside the cemetery toward Nassau.
University Laundry Co. occupies a long building in block 35 on Willow.
G. C. Silcox planing mill is on Branch Avenue.
V. F. Frohling, carpenter and cabinet maker, is in block 35.
50 ft. North points left. Chestnut, Moran Av, Moore, Madison, Willow, Park Pl, Nassau; cemetery in the middle.

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9, at 50 ft to an inch, covers the residential streets north of Nassau, from Chestnut on the west to Linden Lane on the east, with Spruce crossing near the top and Pine and Maple running north from Nassau between them. The blocks are laid out in long narrow lots, many still empty: block 40 between Maple and Linden Lane has only a handful of houses, and the lots above Spruce are largely open. Built lots hold small two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings with sheds, stables and automobile houses, a few flats and a grocery near Nassau. Industry and services are scattered among them. Above Spruce stand the greenhouses, work shop and wagon house of George Allen, florist, heated by hot water, and the small iron-clad brass foundry and machine shop of Leggett and Duryea with a gasoline engine. In block 38 between Chestnut and Pine is Ed. Everets' wood yard with a wood pile and gasoline engine, and on Chestnut the fire house of Princeton Engine Co. No. 1, with a note listing its members and equipment (a steamer, a hose carriage and a reel cart). A row of automobile houses, stables and a wagon shed lines the back of the lots near Nassau. The Nassau frontage holds dwellings rather than shops. Murray Place appears as a stub off Nassau at the bottom edge. A compass rose stands at the upper left and the scale bar at the bottom.
notes: George Allen, florist, has a range of greenhouses north of Spruce.
Leggett and Duryea brass foundry and machine shop stands north of Spruce near Chestnut.
Fire house of Princeton Engine Co. No. 1 (50 members, steamer, hose carriage, reel cart) is on Chestnut.
Ed. Everets' wood yard is in block 38 between Chestnut and Pine.
Block 40 between Maple and Linden Lane is mostly unbuilt lots.
50 ft. Chestnut, Spruce, Pine, Maple, Linden Ln, Nassau.

sheet-10-main.description: The main part of sheet 10, at 100 ft to an inch, covers the open ground on the western edge of the borough between Stockton Street at the top and Morningside Avenue at the bottom, bounded on the west by Lovers Lane (continuing south of Mercer as Olden's Lane) and on the east by Langlotz Avenue. Mercer Street crosses the middle of the part diagonally. The area is thinly built: large estate lots with a handful of detached frame dwellings, several marked stuccoed, a small blue-coloured building in the open ground north of Mercer, a play house, an automobile shed on Olden's Lane, and one dwelling south of Morningside Avenue noted as drawn from plans. The one cluster of buildings is in the north-east corner below Stockton Street: a range of greenhouses with glass roofs, storage and a gas engine house, labelled heated by hot water. A water tank on a steel tower (20 by 60 ft, 142,000 gallons, elevated 60 ft) stands in a small enclosure on the west side of Langlotz Avenue. The dash-dot borough line runs down the centre of Lovers Lane and Olden's Lane and then turns east across the lower part of the sheet, so much of this part lay outside the borough in 1911. Water pipes with their dates of laying are drawn along the streets. Elm Road is drawn only as a stub leaving Stockton Street. A large decorative compass rose fills the empty block in the upper right, beside the 'Aug. 1911 Princeton N.J.' cartouche, and the scale bar sits at the bottom. Neighbouring sheets 20 and 11 adjoin to the west and east.
notes: Morningside Avenue is now Battle Road.
Langlotz Avenue is now Springdale Road.
Olden's Lane is now Olden Lane; Lovers Lane keeps its name.
The borough line follows Lovers Lane and Olden's Lane, then crosses the part eastward north of Morningside Avenue.
Greenhouses heated by hot water in the north-east corner, with a gas engine and storage building.
Water tank 20 by 60 ft, 142,000 gallons, elevated 60 ft on a steel tower, west of Langlotz Avenue.

100 ft. Two parts: Prospect Av strip (eating clubs, anchored on Prospect/Washington Rd) west of heavy line at overview x~490; main (Lovers Ln, Mercer, Morningside=Battle Rd, Stockton, Langlotz=Springdale Rd).

sheet-10-prospect.description: The western strip of sheet 10, cut off from the main map by a heavy vertical line, shows the east side of Prospect Avenue between Washington Road and a point beyond Olden Street, drawn at 100 ft to an inch and turned on the page: Prospect Avenue runs up the sheet, with its own north arrow pointing to the upper left. Only the lots on the east side of the avenue are drawn; the west side belongs to sheets 14 and 15, and Olden Street is shown only as a short stub entering from the left. The strip is the row of Princeton University eating clubs. From Washington Road northward the lots are labelled Campus Club, Tower Club, Terrace Club, Cannon Club, Quadrangle Club, Ivy Club, Cottage Club and Cap and Gown Club, then, beyond Olden Street, Charter Club and Key and Seal Club. Ivy, Cottage, Cap and Gown and Campus are coloured as brick, Cannon Club as stone and the rest as frame; Ivy has a separate servants' quarters behind it and a lockers building stands at the rear of one of the lots north of Cap and Gown. Between the clubs are several frame dwellings, and three unlabelled frame houses occupy the lots at the northern end of the strip. House numbers are marked along the avenue frontage. Water pipes with their dates of laying (1881, 1892, 1907) are drawn in Prospect Avenue and Washington Road, with fire alarm boxes at Olden Street and at Washington Road. Block number 45 is marked on a curved lot line behind Cap and Gown Club.
notes: Turned part: Prospect Avenue runs up the page, with a separate north arrow pointing to the upper left.
Eating clubs labelled: Campus, Tower, Terrace, Cannon, Quadrangle, Ivy, Cottage, Cap and Gown, Charter, Key and Seal.
Only the east side of Prospect Avenue is drawn; the west side is on sheets 14 and 15.

100 ft. Two parts: Prospect Av strip (eating clubs, anchored on Prospect/Washington Rd) west of heavy line at overview x~490; main (Lovers Ln, Mercer, Morningside=Battle Rd, Stockton, Langlotz=Springdale Rd).

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11, at 100 ft to an inch, covers the south-west side of the borough between Stockton Street along the top and the borough line near the bottom, from Langlotz Avenue on the west to Alexander Street on the east. Mercer Street crosses the sheet diagonally from the lower left to the upper right, and Edgehill Street and Library Place run south from Stockton Street to it. North of Mercer Street the blocks along Edgehill Street and Library Place are residential, with two- and three-storey frame dwellings, some brick houses, carriage and automobile houses and a painting and wood-working shop at the south end of Edgehill Street. At the upper right is Thompson Park, with Thompson Hall, a branch of the public library, and the small stone Borough Hall on Mercer Street. The Theological Seminary of the Presbyterian Church occupies the ground between Library Place, Mercer Street and Alexander Street and continues south of Mercer: the seminary Library and Old Library, Alexander Hall, Miller Chapel, Hodge Hall, Stuart Hall, the Gymnasium, Brown Hall and a power house with three engines, three dynamos, a coal house and a 100 ft chimney, with a printed note on the watchman and fire service. Mercer Street west of the seminary is lined with numbered frame dwellings. Stockton Place leaves Alexander Street westward with a few dwellings, barns and a workshop. The large lower half is mostly open: the Princeton Graduate College (Thompson College, drawn from plans), with Proctor Hall and the 165 ft Cleveland Tower, stands near the borough line, and a Golf Club building is drawn just below the line. A compass rose fills the open ground at the left.
notes: Princeton Graduate College (Thompson College) with Proctor Hall and Cleveland Tower (165 ft) is drawn from plans.
Thompson Hall in Thompson Park is labelled as a branch of the public library; Borough Hall stands at its corner on Mercer Street.
Seminary buildings labelled: Library, Old Library, Alexander Hall, Miller Chapel, Hodge Hall, Stuart Hall, Gymnasium, Brown Hall; power house with 3 engines and 3 dynamos.
The borough line crosses the lower part of the sheet; the Golf Club building lies outside it.
The scan has a misaligned band across the sheet just above Mercer Street, where parts of the drawing are repeated or offset.
100 ft. Mercer, Stockton, Alexander, Stockton Pl (=College Rd), Langlotz (=Springdale Rd); seminary grounds. 1911 Library Pl about 50 m off the modern one, left out.
placenames: Theological Seminary of the Presbyterian Church

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12, drawn at 50 ft to an inch, covers the blocks south of the western end of Nassau Street, where Stockton Street and Mercer Street meet it, and runs south to Dickinson Street, between Alexander Street on the west and University Place on the east. Bayard Street and Bank Street are drawn only as short stubs at the top edge. The point where Mercer Street joins Nassau Street holds a small cluster of shops: hardware, an insurance office, a repair shop with electrical supplies, a clothing store, a drug store, a confectionery with an ice cream factory run by an electric motor, and two upholstering shops. The rest of the sheet is residential. Trinity Episcopal Church, with its Sunday school and parish house and the brick rectory on Stockton Street, fills the block between Stockton and Mercer; a private school and the small stone Trinity Club are nearby. The Nassau Club occupies a brick building on the block between Mercer Street and University Place. The Conover Bros. carriage works, with a blacksmith and wheelwright shop and a paint shop above, stands behind the Mercer Street houses, and near the Alexander Street end of Edwards Place are a blacksmith, a carpenter's shop, a plumber, a tin shop and a three-storey frame grocery. Edwards Place itself is lined on its south side by a long row of twelve attached two-storey frame dwellings. Large frame and some brick dwellings fill the blocks along Alexander Street, Mercer Street and University Place. In the lower left corner, beyond Alexander Street, several large buildings are drawn only in outline and colour without detail; they belong to sheet 11.
notes: Bayard Street is now Bayard Lane.
Trinity Episcopal Church with Sunday school, parish house and rectory; Trinity Club building nearby.
Conover Bros., carriage makers: blacksmith, wheelwright and paint shop, no power or lights.
Nassau Club on the block east of Mercer Street.
Ice cream factory with electric motor behind the shops at Nassau and Mercer.
Buildings in the lower left corner, west of Alexander Street, are shown without detail and are drawn in full on sheet 11.
50 ft. Stockton, Mercer, Alexander, Edwards Pl, University Pl, Dickinson, Nassau. Mercer/Nassau realigned.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13, at 100 ft to an inch, shows the central campus of Princeton University, lettered across the sheet, between Nassau Street at the top, University Place on the west and Washington Road on the east, down to the borough line near the bottom. Only the south side of Nassau Street is drawn; Mercer Street, Chambers Street, John Street, Baker Street, Witherspoon Street and Van Deventer Avenue appear as stubs at the top edge, and Edwards Place, Dickinson Street, William Street and Prospect Avenue as stubs at the sides. Nearly every building is a university building, most coloured as stone: University Hall (offices, dormitories and police headquarters) at the corner of Nassau and University Place, Holder, Hamilton, Campbell and Blair Halls, the Halsted Observatory, Alexander Hall, Reunion Hall, West College, Nassau Hall, the Library, Dickinson Hall, the School of Science with its machine shop and dynamo building, the Biological Laboratory, Clio and Whig Halls, Witherspoon, Edwards and Little Halls, Dodge and Murray Halls, Marquand Chapel, McCosh Hall, Dod Hall, the Art Museum, Brown Hall, Prospect, the '79 Dormitory, the Gymnasium with swimming tank and Brokaw Memorial, Patton Hall and the Ten Class Dormitory, the Infirmary, and the fire-proof Palmer Physical Laboratory and Guyot Hall. The First Presbyterian Church and the Dean's house stand on Nassau Street. The University Power Co. power, heat and light plant adjoins the Gymnasium, and a printed note describes the night watch and fire service. Along the west side, the railroad branch enters from the bottom with several tracks, the railroad station, baggage and express buildings, a freight house and a turntable; small dwellings, a dormitory, a photographer and a trolley shed line University Place, with the Bachelor's Club and a stuccoed Armory beyond. The Vivarium lies just outside the borough line.
notes: Van Deventer Avenue is now Vandeventer Avenue.
John Street and Baker Street, drawn as stubs north of Nassau Street, are not in the modern street data.
Railroad branch with station, baggage house, express office, freight house and turntable on the west side of the campus.
The University Power Co. plant (engines, Curtis turbine and dynamos) adjoins the Gymnasium.
Palmer Physical Laboratory and Guyot Hall are marked as fire-proof construction.
A printed note gives the university watch service: three night watchmen with Newman clocks, city water, hydrants and hose.
The borough line crosses the lower part of the sheet; the Vivarium lies south of it.
100 ft. University campus: Nassau, University Pl, Washington Rd, William, Prospect; railroad (old branch, rail points off).

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14, drawn at 50 ft to an inch, covers two blocks south of Nassau Street between Washington Road on the west and Charlton Street on the east, divided by William Street and bounded at the bottom by Prospect Avenue. Van Deventer Avenue and Moore Street appear as stubs on the far side of Nassau Street. In the north-west corner of the upper block are two Princeton University buildings, both brick: the School of Chemistry and the School of Engineering Laboratory, with an engine, pumps and a 75 ft iron chimney; a note refers to sheet 13 for the university's fire report. The Nassau Street frontage is a row of numbered two- and three-storey frame dwellings, with wagon houses, a livery stable and its office, a tin shop and a crib behind them. The middle of the block holds the brick Model Public School and, beside it, a large new stone and brick Public School drawn from plans. The east end of the block, along Charlton Street, has more frame dwellings and outbuildings. On the south side of William Street stand frame dwellings, a Model School Annex and, at the Charlton Street corner, the Princeton University Press, a large building drawn from plans. The lower block is mostly open ground with a few large houses along Washington Road and Prospect Avenue: a house with an attached observatory, the Washington Inn, a carriage house and, near Charlton Street, the brick Colonial Club, one of the Prospect Avenue eating clubs. Water pipes with their dates, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are marked in the streets. A compass rose sits at the left edge and a scale of feet at the lower left.
notes: Van Deventer Avenue is now Vandeventer Avenue.
Princeton University School of Chemistry and School of Engineering Laboratory at Nassau Street and Washington Road; the university's fire report is on sheet 13.
The Public School beside the Model Public School and the Princeton University Press on William Street are drawn from plans.
The Colonial Club, an eating club, stands on Prospect Avenue near Charlton Street.
A dwelling on Prospect Avenue has an attached observatory.
50 ft. Nassau, Washington Rd, William, Charlton, Prospect Av.

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15, drawn at 50 ft to an inch, covers the ground south of Nassau Street from Charlton Street on the west to beyond Olden Street, down to Prospect Avenue at the bottom. William Street crosses the western half, and Chestnut Street and Pine Street appear as stubs on the far side of Nassau Street. The block between Nassau, Charlton, William and Olden Streets is densely built: numbered two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, many of them double houses, line Nassau, Charlton and William Streets, with a grocery at the Nassau and Charlton corner, two blacksmith shops, coops, wagon sheds and an auto and carriage house beside a livery stable with a gasoline pump and wind mill behind it. South of William Street, Charlton Street is lined with more frame dwellings and a grocery; behind them are the yard of The Reardon Co., contractors, with storage and dilapidated sheds, and Wm. McDonald's automobile storage and stable, while the rest of block 49 is open. Along Prospect Avenue are three eating clubs: the Tiger Inn Club, plastered with a stone first storey, the Elm Club House of plastered frame, and an unnamed club house on Olden Street. East of Olden Street the north block has a few large houses on Nassau Street; everything south of it is the Athletic Field of the Princeton University Athletic Association, with a running track, bleachers on three sides, a grand stand, a gate shed, the Field House and The Cage, a large brick building with a wire-netting skylight roof. Freshmen's Field lies south of the track, with the brick Osborn Club House at the corner of Olden Street and Prospect Avenue. A compass rose is drawn in the middle of the athletic field and a scale of feet at the lower left.
notes: Athletic field with bleachers, grand stand, Field House and The Cage (roof of wire netting and skylights).
Eating clubs on Prospect Avenue: The Tiger Inn Club and The Elm Club House; Osborn Club House at Olden Street.
The Reardon Co., contractors, and Wm. McDonald automobile storage and stable on the Charlton Street block.
Livery stable with gasoline pump and wind mill behind the Nassau Street houses.
A brick building at the lower left edge is drawn without detail; it continues from sheet 14.
50 ft. Nassau, William, Charlton, Olden, Prospect Av; athletic field fills the east half.
placenames: Athletic Field of the Princeton University Athletic Association

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16, at 100 ft to an inch, covers the eastern edge of the borough south of Nassau Street, from Murray Place and Fitz Randolph Road on the west to Harrison Street on the east, down past The Western Way. Maple Street, Linden Lane, Evelyn Place and Ewing Street are drawn as stubs on the far side of Nassau Street. Between Nassau Street and Prospect Avenue the land is laid out in large numbered blocks crossed by Aiken Avenue, Princeton Avenue and Patton Avenue, but it is still thinly built: a few frame dwellings along Murray Place and Nassau Street, much open ground in blocks 55 to 59, and a small house drawn in stone. The Nassau Street frontage at the north-east is denser, with numbered double frame houses, a few brick ones, a carpenter's shop, a grocery at the Ewing Street corner, a brick bakery with its oven and a tin shop behind. Harrison Street runs down the east side, with lots lettered along it and a row of new dwellings of concrete block in its lower part. South of Prospect Avenue a new residential tract is laid out along Fitz Randolph Road, Broadmead and The Western Way, with curving lot lines around small courts and most of its two-and-a-half-storey houses marked stuccoed, along with a stuccoed auto house. Block 61, below The Western Way, is almost empty. Along the left edge the sheet repeats the edge of the athletic field from sheet 15, with part of its grand stand, bleachers and The Cage in outline, and below it a few stuccoed houses on the south side of Prospect Avenue west of Fitz Randolph Road. Water pipes with their dates, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are marked; a compass rose stands in the open ground of block 51 and the scale bar is at the bottom.
notes: Fitz Randolph Road is now Fitzrandolph Road; The Western Way is now Western Way.
Ewing Street, a stub north of Nassau Street opposite Harrison, is where North Harrison Street now runs; the name is not in the modern street data.
Several dwellings on the lower part of Harrison Street are of concrete block.
Most houses in the tract along Fitz Randolph Road, Broadmead and The Western Way are marked stuccoed.
Bakery with oven, grocery and tin shop at the corner of Nassau and Harrison Streets.
100 ft. Nassau, Murray Pl, Aiken, Princeton Av, Patton, Prospect, Broadmead, The Western Way, Harrison. Fitz Randolph Rd and most Harrison junctions realigned, excluded.

sheet-17-west.description: The west part of sheet 17 covers the southern edge of the borough of Princeton along Alexander Street, from Dickinson Street at the top of the sheet south to the borough line at the bottom. Alexander Street runs down the page as the main axis of the part; at the top it bends to the northeast, where it meets Dickinson Street, which crosses the head of the sheet. University Place runs down the east side of the top block as far as a heavy dividing line, and Stockton Place (22 ft wide) leaves Alexander Street to the west about a third of the way down. The block between Dickinson Street, University Place and Alexander Street is lined with two- and three-storey frame dwellings facing Dickinson Street, with small outbuildings, a paint shop and an auto house behind them, and the yard of W. R. Mathews, contractor and builder, with an office and a large open storage area for building material shaded blue. The east side of Alexander Street below this block is a regular row of numbered frame dwellings, with sheds, a wagon shed, two coal sheds behind a stone retaining wall and a bin. The west side is drawn sparsely: a few large houses set back on deep lots, one of them brick, and wide blank areas carrying the block numbers 11 and 44. Water pipes with their sizes and dates of laying, fire alarm boxes and hydrants are marked along the streets. The part is drawn at 50 ft to an inch; the compass rose in the upper left shows north pointing to the upper right. A heavy line separates it from the middle strip of the sheet, which carries the railroad spur and turntable and belongs to other parts.
notes: W. R. Mathews, contractor and builder: office and storage yard for building material on the Dickinson Street block.
The borough line is drawn as a dashed line along the bottom edge of the part.
Water pipe labels give sizes and dates (4 in. water pipe, 1889) along Alexander Street.
Streets carry drawn widths: Alexander 45 to 50 ft at the bend, Stockton Place 22 ft, University Place 50 ft.

50 ft. Three parts: west (Alexander, Dickinson, University Pl, Stockton Pl=College Rd), middle (Alexander, rail spur, turntable) and east strip (coal yard). Middle and east have no junction: not configured.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: Alexander Street further south, rail spur and turntable (no street junction; modern rail cut back and moved; needs step 6b from sheet-6 or sheet-13 features (none found reliable so far)).
Not georeferenced on this sheet: Alexander Street, Conover & Matthews coal yard, Rearden Co. (no street junction; needs step 6b from sheet-6 (adjoins at the bottom right)).

sheet-18-southeast.description: The southeast part of sheet 18 is a detached block on the east side of Princeton: the grounds of the Princeton Preparatory School, between Snowden Lane on the west and Nassau Street at the bottom of the part. Snowden Lane (40 ft) runs up the left side of the part from Nassau Street (65 ft), which crosses the foot of the sheet. The school property fills almost the whole block east of Snowden Lane and is drawn largely empty. Near the top stands a frame school building with a gasoline engine and pump; near the middle a main building made up of a three-storey dormitory, a kitchen wing with a cement floor, and a two-and-a-half-storey dwelling, with a water tank of 5000 gallons. The school's notes read: J. B. Fine, proprietor, 50 students, no watchman, steam heat, electric light, water supply from two open wells with a gasoline engine and pump, 100 ft of rubber hose, four insurance fire extinguishers and no other fire apparatus. A small coal house stands on Snowden Lane, and one dwelling is drawn on the south side of Nassau Street. The words "No exposure" are lettered along the top and right edges of the block, meaning no buildings lay close enough beyond them to matter for fire risk. The part is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, with its own north arrow pointing up and slightly to the right, and carries the sheet's scale bar. The Princeton University Library map division stamp is printed over Nassau Street. A heavy line along the left edge separates it from the southwest part of the sheet.
notes: Princeton Preparatory School, J. B. Fine, proprietor, 50 students: school, dormitory, kitchen and dwelling with a 5000 gallon water tank.
"No exposure" is lettered along the north and east sides of the school grounds.
Library stamp (Map Division, Princeton University Library) printed across Nassau Street.
50 ft. Three parts: top (Bayard Ln, Birch Av, Leigh Av; helmert), southwest (Franklin Av / Witherspoon, north points left; anchored), southeast (Snowden Ln / Nassau; anchored).

sheet-18-southwest.description: The southwest part of sheet 18 shows the area where Franklin Avenue meets Witherspoon Street at the northern end of the Witherspoon Street neighbourhood. The part is drawn turned on the page: its north arrow points to the left, so Witherspoon Street runs across the bottom of the part and Franklin Avenue (50 ft) runs up the page from it. Witherspoon Lane, also lettered Onque Lane, a narrow 15 ft lane, runs up the right side of the part parallel to Franklin Avenue. West of Franklin Avenue lies a dairy farm, owned by Walter B. Harris and leased to J. Golden Pierson, drawn as a frame dwelling with a long line of attached sheds and coops and, scattered across the open ground, barns, wagon houses and a milk house with stove and hot water boiler, marked as having no fire apparatus. Between Franklin Avenue and Witherspoon Lane block 23 holds a row of five two-storey dwellings and several pairs of attached frame houses on the lane, a dwelling partly drawn in the blue of stone, and a group of two-and-a-half-storey double houses facing Witherspoon Street, numbered 123 to 131. A 4 in. water pipe laid in 1895 runs along Witherspoon Street, with a hydrant at the Franklin Avenue corner. The part is drawn at 50 ft to an inch. It is separated from the top part of the sheet by a heavy line along its upper edge and from the southeast part by another along its right edge; the block numbers 4 and 5 of the neighbouring blocks are printed at its foot and right side.
notes: Witherspoon Lane is also lettered "(Onque Lane)"; the modern name is Witherspoon Lane.
Dairy farm of Walter B. Harris, owner, J. Golden Pierson, lessee, west of Franklin Avenue; no fire apparatus.
Drawn with north to the left, so Witherspoon Street runs across the page and Franklin Avenue up it.
50 ft. Three parts: top (Bayard Ln, Birch Av, Leigh Av; helmert), southwest (Franklin Av / Witherspoon, north points left; anchored), southeast (Snowden Ln / Nassau; anchored).

sheet-18-top.description: The top part of sheet 18 covers a newly laid-out residential tract on the northwest side of Princeton, between Bayard Lane on the west and the edge of the sheet on the east. A 50 ft trolley right of way crosses the head of the sheet, and below it two parallel streets run across the page: Birch Avenue (50 ft) and Leigh Avenue (40 ft). Bayard Lane (50 ft) runs down the left side at a slight slant and meets both. The blocks are divided into long rows of narrow numbered building lots, with house numbers and lot numbers both shown along Leigh Avenue. Most lots are empty: the block between Birch and Leigh Avenues has only a handful of two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, the block north of Birch Avenue none at all, and the large area between the trolley right of way and Birch Avenue carries only the block number 14. South of Leigh Avenue there is a row of five attached two-storey dwellings, a pair of double houses, a dwelling with brick and stone parts, and at the corner of Bayard Lane a lot with an ice house, a tool house and a coop, with one dwelling set back near the dividing line. The dash-dot borough line runs along Leigh Avenue and then cuts diagonally across the lots south of it. Water pipes of 3/4 in., 1 in. and 4 in. are marked in Bayard Lane and Leigh Avenue. The part is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with north at the top, shown by the compass rose in its lower half. Heavy lines separate it from the two southern parts of the sheet, which are drawn at other orientations.
notes: A trolley right of way, 50 ft wide, is drawn across the top of the sheet with no track or building.
The borough line follows Leigh Avenue and then runs diagonally through the lots south of it.
The scan repeats a narrow strip just below Leigh Avenue: lot numbers 46 to 50 and the outbuilding on lot 53 appear twice, apparently where two scans were joined.
Most of the numbered lots on Birch and Leigh Avenues were still vacant in 1911.
50 ft. Three parts: top (Bayard Ln, Birch Av, Leigh Av; helmert), southwest (Franklin Av / Witherspoon, north points left; anchored), southeast (Snowden Ln / Nassau; anchored).

sheet-19-basin.description: The inset in the upper right of sheet 19 is a detached view of the Delaware and Raritan Canal at the road from Princeton, noted as located 1 1/4 miles south of the post office. It is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, framed by heavy lines, and has no streets other than the road itself. The road, lettered Road to Princeton and 38 ft wide, runs up the page and crosses the canal on a bridge at the bottom of the inset; this is the line of the modern Alexander Street and Alexander Road. The canal is drawn as a band of blue water running across the foot of the inset, interrupted by the bridge, and lettered D. & R. Canal. The one substantial building is the former grist mill of Berrien & Warren on the west side of the road just north of the canal: a two-and-a-half-storey brick building with a one-storey frame addition at its south end and sheds along the road, marked vacant, with the note that all buildings are vacant and dilapidated. A small vacant brick building and a frame shed stand by the road at the top of the inset. The rest of the inset is blank. The inset has no north arrow of its own; the compass rose just below its lower edge belongs to the south part of the sheet.
notes: The canal is lettered "D. & R. Canal".
The road lettered "Road to Princeton" is the modern Alexander Street and Alexander Road, crossing the canal on a bridge.
Former Berrien & Warren's grist mill: all buildings vacant and dilapidated.
Inset located, by its own note, 1 1/4 miles south of the post office.

Three parts: north (100 ft; Linden Ln, Spruce, Evelyn Pl, Ewing=N Harrison, Nassau), south (50 ft; Wiggins, Greenview, Humbert, Jefferson, Moore; helmert) and inset at Princeton Basin (Alexander St at the D&R Canal; 50 ft, hand-placed).

sheet-19-north.description: The north part of sheet 19 covers the north side of Nassau Street on the eastern edge of Princeton, from Linden Lane on the west to beyond Ewing Street on the east, reaching north to Spruce Street. It is drawn at 100 ft to an inch, half the scale of the rest of the sheet, with its own scale bar and a north arrow pointing up. Nassau Street runs across the foot of the part, with the mouths of Princeton Avenue and Harrison Street on its south side. Linden Lane runs up the left side to Spruce Street, which crosses the top corner; Evelyn Place is a short street running north from Nassau Street and ending in a turning circle; and Ewing Street runs north from the Harrison Street corner across the whole part. The Nassau Street frontage is lined with frame dwellings, a few of brick, numbered 280 to 380, with stables, coops and auto houses behind them. Along Linden Lane the lots are small and numbered 3 to 14, with a few dwellings and a plumbing and tin shop. Behind the frontage the land is open: large irregular lots with scattered dwellings, a barn, coops, and a dwelling partly of stone, in blocks 52 and 53. A stone quarry is lettered in the open ground east of Ewing Street near the top of the sheet. Water pipes, including a 6 in. pipe in Nassau Street laid in 1897 and a 4 in. pipe in Linden Lane, hydrants and a fire alarm box at Harrison Street are marked. A heavy line along the bottom separates the part from the inset and the south part of the sheet, and the block number 16 is printed across the south side of Nassau Street.
notes: Drawn at 100 ft to an inch with its own scale bar; the south part and the inset of the same sheet are at 50 ft.
Stone quarry lettered in the open land east of Ewing Street.
Evelyn Place ends at a turning circle north of Nassau Street.
Plumbing and tin shop on Linden Lane.
Water pipe in Nassau Street labelled as laid in 1897; Linden Lane pipe labelled 1903 and 1910.

Three parts: north (100 ft; Linden Ln, Spruce, Evelyn Pl, Ewing=N Harrison, Nassau), south (50 ft; Wiggins, Greenview, Humbert, Jefferson, Moore; helmert) and inset at Princeton Basin (Alexander St at the D&R Canal; 50 ft, hand-placed).

sheet-19-south.description: The south part of sheet 19 covers the blocks north of Wiggins Street in the Witherspoon Street neighbourhood of Princeton, between Greenview Avenue on the west and Moore Street on the east. Wiggins Street runs across the foot of the part, with the mouths of Vandeventer Avenue, Madison Street and Hamilton Avenue on its south side. Greenview Avenue, also lettered Cemetery, runs up the left edge, and the word Cemetery is lettered along the boundary of the cemetery beyond its upper end. Humbert Street, also lettered New, runs up the middle of the part, and Jefferson Road and Moore Street run north from Wiggins Street on the right, either side of an almost empty block carrying the compass rose and the block number 2. The blocks are densely built with two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, many of them double houses, with a few of brick and stone. Among them are a bakery with an oven and a bake house, a grocery, an iron-clad plumbing and tin shop with a stock room, a work shop, sheds, coops and a wagon shed, and the sash and blind works of E. M. Updike, a sawing and planing mill driven by a gasoline engine, with no lights, stove heat and no fire apparatus. Large frame dwellings face Wiggins Street, and a house foundation is drawn on Jefferson Road. Water pipes with dates of laying from 1900 to 1911, hydrants and a fire alarm box at Hamilton Avenue are marked. The part is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the sheet's scale bar and the Princeton University Library stamp at the bottom right. Heavy lines separate it from the 100 ft north part and from the canal inset in the upper right.
notes: Greenview Avenue is also lettered "(Cemetery)"; the modern name is Greenview Avenue.
Humbert Street is also lettered "(New)"; the modern name is Humbert Street.
Van Deventer Avenue is the modern Vandeventer Avenue.
E. M. Updike, manufacturer of sash and blinds: sawing and planing mill with gasoline engine and underground gasoline tank.
A house foundation without a building is drawn on Jefferson Road.
Jefferson Road water pipe labelled as laid in 1911, the year of the sheet.

Three parts: north (100 ft; Linden Ln, Spruce, Evelyn Pl, Ewing=N Harrison, Nassau), south (50 ft; Wiggins, Greenview, Humbert, Jefferson, Moore; helmert) and inset at Princeton Basin (Alexander St at the D&R Canal; 50 ft, hand-placed).

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 covers the outlying estate country southwest of Princeton, mostly outside the borough line, from Elm Road and Lovers Lane at the top down to Stony Brook at the bottom. It is drawn at 200 ft to an inch, the smallest scale in the atlas, and shows only buildings and property names on large open tracts. Stockton Street runs down the middle of the sheet from the Elm Road corner, curving and crossing Stony Brook on a bridge; Mercer Street runs diagonally down the right half to meet the Stony Brook road near the bottom right corner. Lovers Lane and Olden's Lane cross the top of the sheet, with Morningside Avenue leaving Olden's Lane to the north. In the upper left are Constitution Hill, a group of brick houses, and the grounds of Junius S. Morgan; between Stockton and Mercer Streets lies the large tract of Moses Taylor Pyne with the house Drumthwacket and a group of brick and stuccoed service buildings, greenhouses, a rubbish kiln and buried gasoline tanks. Along Olden's Lane are Peep O'Day (Katherine E. Turnbull) and Maple Hill Farm (C. H. Olden), with a windmill and pump house. East of Mercer Street are Mercer Manor (Henry B. Owsley) and a farm group with barn, dairy and a Rider-Ericsson engine and pump. West of Stockton Street lies Edgerstoune, with a large stone dwelling, a brick and frame greenhouse heated by hot water and an auto and carriage house. Near the brook stand the Stony Brook public school, a Presbyterian chapel and an old mill dated 1714, and south of it the estate of Joseph S. Bruere. Stony Brook is drawn as a blue stream with a small island. The large tracts carry the block numbers 503 to 505.
notes: Olden's Lane is the modern Olden Lane.
Estate owners lettered across their land: Junius S. Morgan, Moses Taylor Pyne, Katherine E. Turnbull, C. H. Olden, Henry B. Owsley, Estate of Jos. S. Bruere.
Old mill on Stony Brook beside the Stockton Street bridge, lettered "Old Mill A.D. 1714", of stone and partly vacant.
Stony Brook Public School and a Presbyterian chapel stand near the brook on Stockton Street.
The road lettered "Stony Brook" and the stream lettered "Stony Brook" are different features; the road runs east to Mercer Street north of the stream.
The borough line crosses the upper left of the sheet, follows Lovers Lane and turns north just east of Mercer Street.
200 ft. Outlying southwest: Stockton, Lovers Ln, Mercer Rd, Morningside=Battle Rd, Stony Brook road=Quaker Rd. Sparse.
